description: Like all theropods, Allosaurus have hollow bones, making them light on their (three-toed) feet. Even the laziest Allosaurus loves running, which makes them excellent steeds. They're often solitary creatures, but they can work well with others in a pinch!

Ankylosaurus might not be the fastest steed, but their impressive stamina and strength make them reliable companions. They're said to have a very strong sense of smell, which helps them sniff out their favourite crunchy snacks.

Archaeopteryx are extremely rare dinos that are adored by many for their gorgeous feathers. If you're ever lucky enough to befriend one, they can accompany you on adventures and seek out valuable items and treasure.

Baryonyx are solitary theropods, easily recognised by the heavy claws it wields on each thumb. Once native to rivers and lakes, modern Baryonyx tend to gravitate towards forests, using their claws to nab fragrant fruits and insects.

Carnotaurus are towering theropods, usually found far from civilization, thanks to their solitary nature and tendency to trample through garden beds. Carnotaurus don't have much use for their tiny arms - instead, they use their powerful jaws (and surprisingly strong depth perception) to nab insects and fruits.

Centrosaurus is a small ceratopsian steed, cherished by many for their intricate frill and horns. Often found in forested areas, they make for excellent farmhands, clearing out land and smashing through obstacles with ease.

Ceratosaurus are great steeds, and are most content in their own company. You'll have to travel to reach the hot, dry climates these carnivorous dinosaurs prefer. With their powerful hind legs, Ceratosaurus are wonderful sprinters and make speedy work of exploring.

Don't let their cuteness fool you - Coelophysis are known for startling inexperienced ranchers with their high speed and agility. They're too small to ride, but they'll happily follow you on your adventures, keeping up with even the fastest steeds.

Compsognathus love foraging. They're social creatures, so you'll often find them roaming in packs, sniffing out food together. Compsognathus are too small to ride, but they'll happily help you track down resources in the wild!

Corythosaurus make for trusty steeds and are happiest hanging with the rest of a herd. With their sprinting ability, they make getting from A to B as quick as can be! They prefer a diet of tasty vegetables and have a great sense of smell for sniffing out fragrant treats.

Deinocheirus enjoy a good meal of - well, anything! All kinds of snacks are on the menu for these omnivorous theropods. These pack dinosaurs like to live in forests, converting all that food into energy for use when sprinting at top speed.

Watch where you're stepping! Deinonychus are little raptors with big claws. In the wild, they run in packs, so they'll be happiest if you find them some company for their pen. They're great trackers, too, so they can help you find other dinos when you're out in the wild!

Don't let their size and appearance fool you - Desmatosuchus can move fast! Their strength and sturdy build makes them a popular mount for travelling traders, but these Archosaurs make for great sprinters too!

Dilophosaurus is a quirky and speedy little steed that is admired for its colourful patterns and crests. They're happiest in packs, and love a warm climate. Treat them well and you'll have a goofy, energetic new best friend.
Dimetrodon is a slow-paced synapsid. They're solitary creatures, and too small to be a steed, but they'll happily keep you company when you're out on adventures.

Like other Ankylosaurids, Euoplocephalus has a broad and flat low torso, and stands on short legs. These introverted dinosaurs like to spend time alone, and enjoy a vegetarian diet. They are great stompers, using their large frame and weighty tail to flatten anything in their way.

Gallimimus are theropods found throughout Paleo Pines, beloved by ranchers of all ages for their bright plumage and playful nature! They make great steeds, too, thanks to their swift speed, ability to sprint - and how cute they look when they run!

Kentrosaurus are smaller and spikier than their Stegosaur cousins, but don't hold that against them! They're social creatures, known for travelling in herds, and make for wonderful company once befriended. You'll often find them in the forest, using their keen sense of smell to hunt down fragrant snacks.

Megalosaurus are three-toed theropods renowned for their impressive strength and gentle demeanour. They make a great steed due to their ability to sprint, but many Megalosaurus are just as happy to spend their days lounging on the ranch.

Microraptors are small four-winged theropods. Good things come in small packages, and as their name suggests, Microraptors are the tiniest dinosaurs! Their small size won't hold them back from joining in with any adventures - these raptors are great companions, and like to explore in packs.

Ouranosaurus are big and friendly herbivores, making them the perfect steeds for younger ranchers. The sail on their back helps them cool off in the heat (and show off to other dinos). Ouranosaurus are social creatures, so they're happiest with at least one other large herbivore in their pen.

Oviraptor may be too small to be a steed, but they love to socialise! These adorable theropod dinos are often found in pairs, and prefer to roam in lush woodlands. Easy to please, their omnivore diet means they eat a wide variety of food.

Pachycephalosaurus are friendly and social creatures. They might seem a little bone headed, but don't hold it against them - the hardened dome on their skull lets them smash through even the sturdiest of rocks with ease.

Parasaurolophus are quite the rare sight! These friendly dinosaurs make for loyal, loving companions. They are versatile steeds, capable of travelling long distances and sprinting short ones. The curved bony crest on their head helps them make loud noises - often heard when they've just chowed a delicious treat!

Pinacosaurus may be short, but their long tail and strong legs make them great stomping dinosaurs. Their distinguishing feature are the short spikes that cover their body. Pinacosaurus take a slow and steady approach to life, and make for dependable steeds.

Postosuchus are large and swift archosaurs, often keeping to themselves in the wild. Despite their posture, the front limbs of a Postosuchus rarely touch the ground. They prefer to walk upright instead, using their arms to reach for juicy snacks.

Fans of hot, sunny climates, Protoceratops are found in desert areas. These cute herbivores have a large frill and small horn on their nose. They generally gather in herds, preferring to share their company with lots of little Protoceratops!

Psittacosaurus are adorable little dinos that like to hang out in pairs. They're often found sniffing out fresh vegetables in the wild, or using their beaks to crack open crunchy treats. Amazingly, Psittacosaurus are distant relatives of the Triceratops, but their small size better suits them for tracking than smashing.

Sarcosuchus is a playful and cheeky creature that thrives with friends in warm environments near water. With their sturdy build, this crocodyliform can help smash through any obstacle making them the perfect steed to navigate sweeping landscapes.

The sweet Scelidosaurus may be on the smaller side, but their tough, bony body keeps them safe as they seek out the freshest fruit to keep themselves full. They are most content in the company of a herd and prefer to roam in open grasslands.

Magnificent, semi-aquatic theropods often found frolicking near Veridian Valley's rivers. Don't be scared by the toothy smile... these gentle giants are sweethearts who love exploring, swimming and watering crops.

They might not look like the most comfortable steed, but thanks to their strength and style, Stegosaurus makes for a reliable companion. They can easily slash away brambles or vines that are blocking your path - plus, they'll chomp through any vegetables you offer them in record time.

Styracosaurus are horned herbivores, often found grazing in the fields. Like its ceratopsian relatives such as the Triceratops and Centrosaurus, the Styracosaurus is a friendly rock smasher and farm tiller. They are playful and loyal, and can't resist a juicy treat such as a strawberry or a tomato.

Therizinosaurus are unusual theropods. Unlike their relatives, the Tyrannosaurus Rex, they enjoy a strictly vegetarian diet. These large raptors are most often found in wooded areas, where they use their long wing span to slash through any obstacles in their path.

Triceratops is a large ceratopsian, easily identified by its frill, horns, and love of fresh fruit. They're loyal companions, and make quick work of ploughing fields on the ranch, or clearing paths in the wild.

Troodon are lively theropods that thrive in company. These small dinosaurs love to congregate in forest areas, hunting for juicy snacks. They even have different shapes of teeth that allow them to enjoy a filling omnivore diet!

The king of the dinosaurs! Tyrannosaurus Rex is a large and impressive theropod steed - a rare sight in the wild, and an even rarer sight in towns. Don't be intimidated, though! Once befriended, they make loyal friends and excellent steeds.

Sprinting is a favorite activity for the lively Utahraptor. These medium sized raptors enjoy racing around in packs. Although generally found in hot desert climates, Utahraptors are true explorers and can occasionally be seen visiting the Valley.

Velociraptor is a small raptor companion known for their agility. They love treats and attention, and are happiest when kept in small flocks. Their ancestors were extremely effective hunters, but modern Velociraptors are just as skilled at tracking down rare resources and materials!

Wuerhosaurus enjoy a slower pace of life, similar to their Stegosaurus relatives. These large steeds love slashing their way through the undergrowth on the search for delicious veggies. They're also happy to help with harvesting fresh crops on the farm.
